name: Big O Notation
description: Big O notation describes the upper bound on an algorithm's resource usage (time or space) as input size grows. It lets us compare algorithms independently of hardware.
beginnerExplanation: Think of Big O as a speed label for an algorithm. O(1) means instant regardless of how much data you have. O(n) means it takes proportionally longer as data grows. O(n²) means it gets very slow very fast. Big O ignores constants and small terms because we care about the general shape of growth, not exact numbers.
mentalModel: Imagine timing how long it takes to find your phone in a room of n people. If you instantly check your pocket: O(1). If you check each person one by one: O(n). If every person checks every other person: O(n²).
learningObjectives: Understand what Big O notation measures (worst-case growth rate)
Recognize common complexity classes: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ)
Drop constants and lower-order terms when simplifying
Know which DS operations have which complexity

workedExample.title: Classify a Double Loop
workedExample.body: Given arr of size n, a double for-loop runs n × n = n² iterations. The inner body is O(1). Total = O(n²). If a second single loop follows, it's O(n² + n) = O(n²) after simplification.

visualWalkthrough: n=4: O(1)≈1 op, O(n)=4 ops, O(n²)=16 ops
n=16: O(n)=16, O(n²)=256 — already 16× worse
O(2ⁿ) at n=30 = 1 billion — completely impractical

complexityReasoning.body: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(n³) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!). Algorithms above O(n log n) are generally unacceptable for large inputs.

edgeCases: O(n + m) when two separate inputs are involved (e.g., graph problems)
Amortized O(1) can hide occasional expensive operations (e.g., array resize)
Best/average/worst cases may differ dramatically (e.g., quicksort O(n log n) avg vs O(n²) worst)
revisionPrompts: What is the Big O of accessing element i in an array?
Which loop structure gives O(n log n)?
Can O(100n) ever beat O(n²) for small n?

theory: What does O(1) mean, and give two real data structure operations that are O(1)?
Why do we drop constants in Big O? Is O(5n) different from O(n)?
What is the total complexity of a function that has an O(n log n) section followed by an O(n²) section?
practice.coding: Write a function that takes a sorted array and a target value and returns the index using binary search. Analyze and state its time and space complexity.
practice.interview: Your interviewer shows you O(n) vs O(n log n) for a sorting variant. The constant for O(n log n) is 1 and for O(n) is 50. At what value of n does O(n log n) become worse? What does this tell you about Big O in practice?

name: Time Complexity
description: Time complexity measures how the running time of an algorithm scales with input size n. Use it to predict whether your code will be fast enough in production.
beginnerExplanation: Counting how many 'steps' an algorithm takes as a function of input size n. We care about worst-case because that's what determines production SLAs. A single for loop is O(n). Two nested loops are O(n²). Each halving step (like binary search) is O(log n).
mentalModel: Imagine a recipe that works on n ingredients. Doing one thing to each ingredient is O(n). Doing every pair of ingredients is O(n²). Repeatedly splitting the work in half is O(log n).
learningObjectives: Count basic operations per line of code
Identify loops, recursive calls, and their multiplicative effect
Distinguish worst/best/average case
Recognize common patterns: single loop = O(n), nested loops = O(n²), divide-and-halve = O(log n)

workedExample.title: Analyze a Function Step by Step
workedExample.body: def find_max(arr): max_val = arr[0] # O(1); for x in arr: # n iterations;   if x > max_val: max_val = x # O(1) per iteration; return max_val # O(1). Total: O(1) + O(n) * O(1) + O(1) = O(n).

visualWalkthrough: Line 1: max_val = arr[0] — O(1), executes once
Line 2: for x in arr — the loop iterates n times
Line 3: if x > max_val — O(1) comparison, n times total = O(n)
Line 5: return — O(1). Grand total: O(n)

complexityReasoning.body: When loops are nested (outer n times, inner n times), multiply: O(n²). When sections are sequential, add then simplify: O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²). Recursive calls expand into T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) — use the Master Theorem to solve.

edgeCases: A loop that runs from 0 to sqrt(n) is O(√n)
Two separate sequential loops: O(n) + O(m) = O(n + m)
Early return via break: worst case still O(n) unless guaranteed early exit
revisionPrompts: What is the time complexity of checking if an element exists in a sorted array?
Two nested loops where the inner runs from j to n: what is the complexity?
A function that calls itself twice on n/2: what recurrence is this?

theory: What is the time complexity of a function with one loop inside another where the inner loop runs from 0 to i (not 0 to n)?
Distinguish between best, worst, and average case complexity with an example.
practice.coding: Write a function to check if an array has any duplicates. Implement two versions: one O(n²) using nested loops, and one O(n) using a hash set.
practice.interview: Given two algorithms — one O(n log n) and one O(n²) — when would you choose the O(n²) one? What factors beyond Big O matter in production?

name: Space Complexity
description: Space complexity measures the extra memory an algorithm uses beyond the input itself, as a function of input size n.
beginnerExplanation: Space complexity counts how much extra RAM your algorithm allocates. If you create a new array of size n, that's O(n) space. Recursion uses the call stack — each call frame is O(1) but k recursive calls = O(k) stack space. In-place algorithms like in-place quicksort use O(log n) stack space for recursion but O(1) extra data structures.
mentalModel: Think of space complexity as the number of sticky notes you need to solve the problem. If you can solve it on your fingers: O(1). If you need one note per element: O(n). If you need a table of all pairs: O(n²).
learningObjectives: Calculate auxiliary space: space used beyond the input itself
Account for recursive call stack depth
Recognize in-place (O(1) space) vs copy-based (O(n) space) algorithms
Understand space-time tradeoffs (memoization, caching)

workedExample.title: Reverse an Array — Two Approaches
workedExample.body: Approach 1 (O(n) space): Create result = [], push elements in reverse, return result. Approach 2 (O(1) space): Use two pointers, swap arr[left] and arr[right] moving inward. Same time complexity O(n), but very different space usage.

visualWalkthrough: O(1): only 2 pointer variables created regardless of n
O(n): new array of size n allocated
O(log n): binary search recursion depth = log n stack frames
O(n): merge sort needs O(n) auxiliary for the merged halves

complexityReasoning.body: Recursive algorithms pay O(depth) in stack space. Iterative replacements using an explicit stack are equivalent but make the space cost explicit. Memoization trades O(n) space for O(n) time savings.

edgeCases: Input space vs auxiliary space — Big O usually refers to auxiliary space
Tail-call optimization can reduce O(n) stack to O(1) in some languages
Hash maps for deduplication trade O(n) space for O(1) average lookup
revisionPrompts: What is the space complexity of a recursive Fibonacci without memoization?
How does the call stack contribute to space complexity?
Give an example of a space-time tradeoff.

theory: What is the difference between input space and auxiliary space?
What is the space complexity of an iterative vs recursive binary search?
practice.coding: Implement a function to find all duplicates in an array of integers where 1 ≤ a[i] ≤ n. Do it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (use the array itself as a hash map by sign-flipping).
practice.interview: You need to check if a string is a palindrome. Compare the two-pointer O(1) space approach against reversing the string. When does O(1) space actually matter in production?

name: Trie — Prefix Search

complexity.time: O(L) per query where L = word length
complexity.space: O(N × Σ) where N = words, Σ = alphabet size

description: A Trie (Prefix Tree) is a tree where each node represents a character. Insert/search/prefix queries all run in O(L) time — far faster than hash table for prefix matching.
beginnerExplanation: A Trie organizes words character by character in a tree. Each path from root to a marked node spells out a word. Searching for a word 'car' means following root→c→a→r. If the r node is marked as an end, 'car' exists. If not, it doesn't. Prefix matching (startsWith) just checks if root→c→a→r exists at all, without checking the end marker.
mentalModel: Think of a trie as a filing cabinet where each drawer level corresponds to a letter position. To find all words starting with 'ca', open the 'c' drawer, then the 'a' sub-drawer — everything inside are matches.
learningObjectives: Implement TrieNode with children array/map and isEnd flag
Insert a word in O(L) time
Search for a word in O(L) time
Check prefix existence with startsWith in O(L) time
Apply tries to autocomplete and word search problems

workedExample.title: Insert and Search 'card', 'care', 'cat'
workedExample.body: Insert 'card': root→c→a→r→d (mark d.end=true). Insert 'care': root→c→a→r→e (mark e.end=true). Insert 'cat': root→c→a→t (mark t.end=true). Search 'car': root→c→a→r exists but r.end=false → 'car' not in trie. startsWith('ca'): root→c→a both exist → true.

visualWalkthrough: root: {c: ...}
root→c→a→r→d (end), e (end)
root→c→a→t (end)
startsWith('car') = traverse root→c→a→r → true (node exists)

complexityReasoning.body: Each insert/search traverses at most L nodes where L = word length. Space is proportional to total characters across all words, not words² — better than naive string comparisons.

edgeCases: Empty string insertion: just mark root.isEnd = true
Duplicate insertions: idempotent — second insert does nothing new
Case sensitivity: decide upfront whether to lowercase all inputs
revisionPrompts: Why is a trie better than a hash set for prefix queries?
What is the space complexity of a trie with n words each of length L?
How would you implement delete in a trie?

theory: Why does a trie guarantee O(L) search where L is the word length, independent of the number of words stored?
How would you modify a Trie to support wildcard matching (e.g., 'c.r' matches 'car' or 'cor')?
practice.coding: Implement a Trie that supports insert(word), search(word), startsWith(prefix), and an autocomplete(prefix) method that returns all words with that prefix.
practice.interview: Design an autocomplete system for a search engine. How does a Trie help? How would you rank suggestions by frequency? At what scale would you switch from an in-memory Trie to a distributed solution?

name: Master Theorem
description: The Master Theorem provides a formula to solve recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), covering divide-and-conquer algorithms like merge sort, binary search, and Strassen's matrix multiplication.
beginnerExplanation: When an algorithm splits work into 'a' subproblems of size 'n/b' and does f(n) extra work at each level, use the Master Theorem. Compare f(n) to n^(log_b(a)). If f(n) is smaller: subproblem work dominates → O(n^log_b(a)). If they're equal: log factor kicks in → O(n^log_b(a) · log n). If f(n) is larger: extra work dominates → O(f(n)).
mentalModel: Imagine splitting a problem into parts (a parts each of size n/b) and doing housekeeping work f(n) at each split level. The Master Theorem tells you who costs more: the subproblems or the housekeeping.
learningObjectives: Identify the a, b, and f(n) in a recurrence
Compute n^log_b(a) and compare to f(n)
Apply all three cases of the Master Theorem
Recognize Merge Sort, Binary Search, Strassen as examples

workedExample.title: Merge Sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)
workedExample.body: a=2, b=2, f(n)=O(n). n^log_2(2) = n^1 = n. f(n) = n = n^1 → Case 2 applies → T(n) = O(n log n).

visualWalkthrough: Binary Search: T(n)=T(n/2)+1 → a=1,b=2,f(n)=O(1). n^log2(1)=n^0=1. f(n)=1=n^0 → Case 2 → O(log n)
Merge Sort: T(n)=2T(n/2)+n → a=2,b=2,f(n)=n. n^log2(2)=n. f(n)=n → Case 2 → O(n log n)
Strassen: T(n)=7T(n/2)+n² → a=7,b=2. n^log2(7)≈n^2.81. f(n)=n² < n^2.81 → Case 1 → O(n^2.81)

complexityReasoning.body: Master Theorem Case 1: f(n) = O(n^(log_b(a) - ε)) for ε > 0. Case 2: f(n) = Θ(n^log_b(a)). Case 3: f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b(a) + ε)) and regularity condition. The theorem does NOT apply to T(n) = T(n-1) + n type recurrences.

edgeCases: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) — Master Theorem does NOT apply (not n/b subdivision)
When a < 1 the theorem doesn't apply (can't have fractional subproblems)
Floors and ceilings in n/b don't affect the asymptotic result
revisionPrompts: Apply the Master Theorem to T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n
Why can't you use the Master Theorem for T(n) = T(n-1) + n?
What is the complexity of Strassen's matrix multiplication and what theorem gives you that?

theory: Solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n using the Master Theorem. Which case applies?
Why doesn't the Master Theorem apply to T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)?
practice.coding: Implement a recursive matrix multiplication. Then implement Strassen's algorithm conceptually (split into 7 recursive calls on n/2 matrices). State the recurrence and apply the Master Theorem.
practice.interview: Your teammate wrote a recursive algorithm with T(n) = 3T(n/3) + O(n). What is its complexity? How does it compare to T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) (merge sort)?

name: Amortized Analysis
description: Amortized analysis gives the true average cost per operation in a sequence, accounting for occasional expensive operations spread over many cheap ones. Critical for understanding dynamic arrays, union-find, and hash tables.
beginnerExplanation: Some operations are expensive rarely, but cheap almost always. Amortized analysis asks: 'If I do n operations total, what's the average cost each?' Dynamic array append is the classic example. 99% of appends are O(1). But when the array fills, we pay O(n) to double capacity. Spread across n appends: total cost = O(n), amortized cost per append = O(1).
mentalModel: Think of a bank account. Every cheap operation deposits $1 of credit. When an expensive operation hits, you withdraw from accumulated savings. If the balance never goes negative, every operation is amortized O(1).
learningObjectives: Understand what amortized analysis measures and when to use it
Apply aggregate analysis: total cost / n operations
Recognize O(1) amortized data structures: dynamic array, stack with multipop
Understand why hash table operations are O(1) amortized

workedExample.title: Dynamic Array Append — Aggregate Analysis
workedExample.body: Start capacity=1. n appends total. Each regular append: O(1). Resize at capacity 1,2,4,8,...,n: costs 1+2+4+...+n = 2n-1 = O(n) total resize cost. n cheap appends add n cost. Total = n + 2n = 3n = O(n) for n operations. Amortized per operation = O(1).

visualWalkthrough: Push 1: cap=1, size=1. Cost=1
Push 2: resize! cap→2, copy 1 element. Cost=2. Push: cost=1. Total=3 for 2 ops → avg=1.5
Push 3,4: resize! cap→4, copy 2. Cost=3. Push 3: 1. Push 4: 1. Running total=8 for 4 ops → avg=2
After n ops: total cost ≤ 3n → amortized O(1) per op

complexityReasoning.body: The trick: each element is copied at most log n times (once per doubling). Total copies = n · log? No — actually sum of geometric series 1+2+4+...+n/2 = n-1. So total work = O(n) for all resizes.

edgeCases: Deletion from dynamic array is also O(1) amortized if we halve at 1/4 capacity
Python list.append() is O(1) amortized for this exact reason
Union-Find with path compression has amortized O(α(n)) ≈ O(1) per operation
revisionPrompts: What is the amortized cost of append to a dynamic array?
If you pop from an expensive-resize-capable stack, is it O(1) amortized?
How does path compression in Union-Find achieve near-O(1) amortized?

theory: Explain amortized analysis using the aggregate method for a dynamic array that doubles in capacity.
Is amortized O(1) the same as average O(1)? What's the difference?
practice.coding: Implement a stack that supports push, pop, and getMin in O(1) amortized time. (Hint: maintain a secondary stack for minimums.)
practice.interview: Python's list.append() is O(1) amortized. Your interviewer asks: 'When would append be slow?' How do you answer, and how would you design a system to avoid this latency spike in real-time applications?
